summary: Clarifies when SIP header fields must use the name-addr form rather than addr-spec. The rule was copied as prose in several places and missed in one. It states the constraint generically for all such header fields, updating RFC 3261 and several extension RFCs.

eli5.summary: A rule about how to write addresses was copied many times and missed once. This writes it down once for all.

questions: when to use name-addr in sip
what is the name-addr form in sip
when must i use name-addr in sip headers
why does sip require angle brackets for certain characters
subtitle: Clarifying when SIP headers must use the formal address format.

tldr.problem: A rule about which format to use for URIs in SIP headers was written into each header's definition separately, making it easy to miss. One header field was indeed missed, and extensions did not consistently include the rule.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC states the rule once, generically: whenever a SIP header field allows choosing between a bare URI (addr-spec) and a named URI (name-addr), use the named form if the URI contains a comma, question mark, or semicolon.
tldr.outcome: All SIP header fields now have the same clear rule, eliminating ambiguity and preventing misinterpretation of headers.

today: RFC 8217 updates RFC 3261 and eight other standards documents to ensure the name-addr rule is consistently applied across all SIP header fields that offer the choice. The constraint is now documented uniformly.

sections.title: The Problem with Split Rules
sections.content:
RFC 3261 defines SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) header fields that contain URIs. These headers allow two ways to write the URI: a bare URI (called addr-spec) or a named URI with angle brackets (called name-addr). For example, the From header can be either sip:alice@example.com or Alice <sip:alice@example.com>.

RFC 3261 included a constraint: if the URI contains a comma, question mark, or semicolon, the named form must be used. This constraint was written separately for each header that has the choice. Because it was repeated instead of stated once, the rule was missed in at least one header definition, and later extension specifications did not consistently include it.
sections.eli5: A rule was written in many places in the handbook, but people still forgot to follow it in one place. Now it is written once at the start.

sections.title: Why Special Characters Need the Named Form
sections.content:
When a SIP message is parsed, a parser reads the header field and stops at certain punctuation marks (commas, semicolons, question marks). If a URI contains these characters and is not enclosed in angle brackets, the parser will split the URI at the wrong place, breaking it into separate values or parameters.

For instance, a bare URI sip:alice@example.com,bob@example.com looks like two addresses separated by a comma. With the named form <sip:alice@example.com,bob@example.com>, the angle brackets tell the parser to treat the entire thing as one URI.
sections.eli5: Special marks mean 'stop here' to a reader. Parentheses tell the reader to keep going and read everything inside as one thing.

sections.title: The Generic Rule
sections.content:
This RFC updates RFC 3261 with a single, clear rule: When a SIP header field grammar allows choosing between addr-spec and name-addr (such as in (name-addr / addr-spec)), the addr-spec form MUST NOT be used if its value contains a comma, semicolon, or question mark.

This rule applies to all such header fields. The headers defined in RFC 3261 that allow this choice are: To, From, Contact, and Reply-To.
sections.eli5: If your address label has special marks in it, put parentheses around it. That is the rule for all address fields.

sections.title: Effect on Extension Headers
sections.content:
The RFC also updates nine other standards documents that define SIP extension header fields. Each extension (such as the Refer method, Referred-By mechanism, and others) adds one or more header fields that use the same addr-spec / name-addr choice. All of these extension header fields are now subject to the same rule.

The updates preserve the status of those RFCs (Standards Track or Informational) but add a note that the constraint applies to them.
sections.eli5: The same rule now applies to extra headers added by other documents, so they all follow the same pattern.

sections.title: Why Clarity Matters
sections.content:
Messages formed without honoring the constraint are still syntactically valid according to the grammar, but they will likely be misinterpreted. Characters after the comma, question mark, or semicolon will be read as header field parameters or additional header values instead of part of the URI. This misinterpretation can cause the message to be sent to the wrong destination or to have the wrong meaning, leading to routing errors or security issues.

The RFC emphasizes that implementations must follow the constraint to prevent these problems.
sections.eli5: Breaking the rule does not make the message invalid, but it will be read the wrong way, which is worse.
